explanation.text: The HTTP POST method is not classified as a safe method in the June 2022 HTTP standard (RFC 9110).
RFC 9110 explicitly lists POST among methods that are not safe, in contrast to methods like GET and HEAD which are defined as safe.
Section 9 of RFC 9110 classifies POST as having no safety property, confirming it is not a safe method.
RFC 9110, published in June 2022, is the authoritative standard defining HTTP semantics, including the classification of methods as safe or unsafe.
The definition of safe methods in RFC 9110 excludes POST, as safe methods are those intended to have no side effects on the server.
POST is defined in RFC 9110 as a method for submitting data to be processed, which implies intended side effects and thus unsafe behavior.

excerpts.text:
RFC 9110 section 9 defines eight methods and classifies each as safe (read only in intent) and idempotent (repeating it has the same intended effect as sending it once):

| Method | Purpose | Safe | Idempotent |
| POST | Resource specific processing of the request content | no | no |

assessment.rationale: RFC 9110, published in June 2022, defines HTTP semantics. Section 9.2.1 (referenced in span 157) states that safe methods are those that do not have side effects, and POST is not among them. The document obsoletes prior versions and confirms POST as unsafe.
assessment.provenance_note: RFC 9110 is an Internet Standard published by IETF in 2022, making it the authoritative source for HTTP semantics at that time.

excerpts.text: This document updates RFC 3864 and obsoletes RFCs 2818, 7231, 7232, 7233, 7235, 7538, 7615, 7694, and portions of 7230.[¶](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#section-abstract-2)
Copyright (c) 2022 IETF Trust and the persons identified as the document authors.

HTTP semantics include the intentions defined by each request method ([Section 9](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#methods)), extensions to those semantics that might be described in request header fields, status codes that describe the response ([Section 15](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#status.codes)), and other control data and resource metadata that might be given in response fields.[¶](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#section-1.3-3)

For example, though the URI of a resource might imply semantics that are not safe, a client can expect the resource to avoid actions that are unsafe when processing a request with a safe method (see [Section 9.2.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#safe.methods)).[¶](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#section-3.1-2)
